title: Absolute frequency measurement of the $^{40}$Ca$^{+}$ clock transition using a GNSS link to the SI second
authors: M. Guevara-Bertsch, M. K. Joshi, M. I Hussain, R. Blatt, C. F. Roos
abstract: We report the absolute frequency measurement of the $4s$ $ ^{2}S_{1/2}\leftrightarrow 3d$ $^{2}D_{5/2}$ $^{40}$Ca$^{+}$ clock transition with respect to the SI second. To perform this measurement, a link between our laboratory in Innsbruck and the clocks realizing the Coordinated Universal Time at the Physikalisch-Technische Bundesanstalt (PTB) in Braunschweig was installed and characterized using the Global Navigation Satellite System GNSS. The comparison between our clock and the ones at PTB was done using the Precise Point Positioning technique. After the evaluation of the systematic shifts, the measured transition frequency is 411 042 129 776 401.2$\pm$0.6 Hz with a fractional uncertainty of 1.5 $\times$ 10$^{-15}$. The stability of the clock measurements was also corroborated by comparing two different calcium ion clock experiments, which share the clock laser source at our institute. Furthermore, after careful evaluation of the trap-drive induced ac magnetic fields, we estimate ac Zeeman shifts on the $D_{5/2}$ sublevels and reevaluate the Landé g-factor of the $3d$ $^{2}D_{5/2}$ level to be g$_{5/2}= 1.200329(1)$.
summary: This experiment achieved an absolute frequency measurement of the $^{40}	ext{Ca}^{+}$ clock transition with unprecedented precision, linking the laboratory clock to the SI second via a GNSS link. By employing Ramsey spectroscopy across multiple Zeeman transitions and meticulously correcting for systematic shifts, the authors determined the frequency to $1.5 	imes 10^{-15}$ uncertainty. This work significantly advances the field of optical atomic clocks and timekeeping standards.
main_problem: The paper reports on the absolute frequency measurement of the highly precise $^{40}	ext{Ca}^{+}$ clock transition relative to the SI second.
main_result: The measured absolute frequency was determined to be $411,042,129,776,401.2 \pm 0.6 	ext{ Hz}$ with a fractional uncertainty of $1.5 	imes 10^{-15}$.
method: The measurement utilized a Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) link to compare the ion clock frequency against the Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) realized at PTB.
model_or_system: The system involves a $^{40}	ext{Ca}^{+}$ ion trapped in a linear Paul trap, with the clock transition ($4s\ ^2S_{1/2} \leftrightarrow 3d\ ^2D_{5/2}$) probed using Ramsey spectroscopy across six different Zeeman sublevels.
key_observables: Absolute transition frequency, fractional uncertainty, and the revised Landé g-factor for the $	ext{D}_{5/2}$ level.
important_parameters: Fractional uncertainty of $1.5 	imes 10^{-15}$; magnetic field strength ($3.0787 	ext{ G}$); and the systematic shift corrections (e.g., ac-Zeeman shifts).
main_assumptions: The measurement relies on the stability and accuracy of the GNSS link and the precise characterization of systematic shifts, such as those induced by trap-drive RF currents.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the energy level scheme, the six transitions used for systematic cancellation, and the absolute frequency measurements referenced to UTC(PTB) over the measurement campaign period.
paper_structure: The paper details the experimental setup, the methodology involving Ramsey spectroscopy and the GNSS link, presents the systematic error analysis in tables, and concludes with the final absolute frequency measurement and comparison to previous literature.
why_interesting: This work represents a state-of-the-art demonstration of linking fundamental atomic physics measurements (clock transitions) to global time standards using advanced satellite technology, pushing the limits of precision measurement in AMO physics.

Two in- frared lasers at 866 nm and 854 nm pump out the metastable D-states to prevent population trapping. (b) Transitions f1, f2, f3, f4, f5, f6 are probed in order to cancel the linear Zeeman shift, ac-Zeeman shift and the quadrupole shift.
